test.name: A living child missing at both censuses is one missing child, not two
test.description: Re-authored from the retired ut_init_project_wm7 now that gap analysis is question-selection's job, not init-project's. Exercises the living-side de-duplication of the census fertility-gap rule: when a living child is absent from the tree at BOTH the 1900 and 1910 censuses, it is one missing child, not one per census. Here born equals living at both censuses, so there are no deceased children.

input.delegation:
Select and record the next research question for this project.

The 1900 US census records 3 children born to Ellen Brannon and 3 still living. The 1910 US census records 4 children born and 4 still living.

projectPath: <workspace>

judge_context: Should call census_children_gap with motherId I1, projectPath, and both census entries (1900: 3 born/3 living; 1910: 4 born/4 living) before writing a question
The tree holds three children: James (b. 1892) and Catherine (b. 1895), both born before the 1900 census, and Thomas (b. 1904), born between the censuses

The tool reports exactly ONE missing child: living, born on or before the 1900 enumeration and still alive at the 1910 enumeration. It is the SAME child accounting for both censuses' excess, not two different children

Counting it twice -- once as 'missing at 1900' and once as 'missing at 1910' -- and writing two separate questions (or one question describing two missing children) is the failure this test guards, and is a FAIL, not a partial
There are no deceased children: children-born equals children-living at both censuses (3/3 and 4/4), so born minus living is zero. The written question must not invent a deceased target
Do not penalize correct reasoning about which census window the missing living child belongs to; the graded point is that it is counted once, not two
The question's selection_basis should be objective_decomposition (Priority 3 — a missing-child group from census_children_gap), per the skill's priority table
